nameStory: European water-horehound gets its name from its love of wet places and its fuzzy, wrinkled leaves that reminded early botanists of the medicinal herb horehound. The 'European' part of the name distinguishes it from our native American species, though this Old World plant has made itself quite at home in New England's wetlands.
description: European water-horehound is a modest perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall in wet, marshy areas. Like other members of the mint family, it has square stems and opposite leaves, but don't expect a minty smell - this one's more earthy and slightly bitter. Its small white flowers cluster in tight whorls around the stem, creating rings of tiny blooms that are easy to overlook. The plant spreads by underground runners, often forming patches in suitable wetland spots.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-angled when you roll them between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are deeply toothed with a coarse, slightly rough texture and no mint scent when crushed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers arranged in dense whorls (rings) around the stem at leaf joints, each flower barely 1/8 inch across

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems rising from creeping underground runners, often forming small colonies in wet areas

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Four small, dry nutlets develop after flowering, typical of mint family plants

habitat: Look for European water-horehound in wet meadows, marshes, pond edges, and ditches throughout New England's lowlands. It thrives in constantly moist to soggy soils and can tolerate some flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants in areas that stay wet most of the year.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground runners as soil warms, with fresh green leaves appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from July through August, when the small white flower whorls are most visible along the square stems.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and stems begin to yellow and die back, though the plant may stay somewhat green into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground runners, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring.

funFact: Despite being in the mint family, European water-horehound was traditionally used to dye wool and cotton black - earning it the alternate name 'gypsywort' because traveling Romani people supposedly used it to darken their skin to avoid persecution.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with native American bugleweed, but European water-horehound typically has more deeply cut leaf teeth and slightly larger flower clusters. Memory trick: 'European = Extra teeth' on the leaves.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called simply 'bugleweed' in field guides, which can cause confusion since several native Lycopus species share this common name. Always check the scientific name to be sure which bugleweed you're reading about.
compareHints: Compared to native bugleweeds like American bugleweed, European water-horehound tends to have more coarsely toothed leaves and slightly showier flower clusters. Northern bugleweed has much smaller, less noticeable flowers, while sweet bugleweed often grows in drier sites and has a more pleasant scent when crushed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the water horehounds, northern bugleweed is the shortest and most delicate, typically staying under 20 inches tall compared to American bugleweed which can reach 4 feet.
Among the water horehounds in New England, American bugleweed is typically the most robust and tall-growing species.
Among New England's water horehounds, sweet bugleweed stands out for its pleasant mint fragrance and hidden stamens.
Among its water horehound relatives, clasping water horehound is unique for its sessile leaves (botanist speak for "no leaf stalk") that wrap around the stem.
Among New England's water horehounds, taperleaf is distinguished by its notably narrow, lance-shaped leaves that taper dramatically to sharp points.
